contribution: The last step of chapter 1 and the bridge to fusion: wave–particle duality from the single-electron double slit, probability as the meaning of the wave, the de Broglie wavelength, and quantum tunnelling, with model values of how fast it falls with barrier width and with the numbers of the proton–proton barrier in the Sun's core.
learn: explain wave–particle duality with the double-slit experiment and probability.
calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron or a proton.
explain how quantum tunnelling makes fusion possible in the Sun.
prior: Light consists of photons, which are detected one by one, $E = hf$ (chapter *Light as particles: the photoelectric effect*)
Two positive nuclei repel each other, and a slower particle turns back further away (chapter *From Rutherford's nucleus to Bohr's atom*)
Kinetic energy $E_\text{k} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ and momentum $p = mv$ (earlier physics courses)

activities.text: The centre of the Sun is about $15.7$ million kelvins. That sounds extremely hot. But fusion needs two positive nuclei to come almost into contact, and at this temperature the protons are far too slow to push so close against their electric repulsion. By the rules of classical physics, fusion in the Sun should practically never happen; physicists met this puzzle in the 1920s. Yet the Sun has been shining for about $4.6$ billion years.
activities.question: How can protons do something that classical physics says they cannot?

activities.title: Review: how close can a nucleus come?
activities.prompt: In the unit *From Rutherford's nucleus to Bohr's atom*, an alpha particle with $8.3\ \text{MeV}$ turned back about $27\ \text{fm}$ from a gold nucleus. What happens to this closest distance if the alpha particle has *less* kinetic energy?

choices.text: It becomes larger: the particle turns back further away.
choices.feedback: Right. All the kinetic energy turns into electric potential energy $kq_1q_2/d$ at the turning point, so a smaller energy means a larger $d$. Slow particles cannot come close.

choices.text: It becomes smaller: a slow particle stays near the nucleus.
choices.feedback: At the turning point $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = kq_1q_2/d$. A smaller kinetic energy gives a *larger* $d$: a slow particle is turned back earlier.

choices.text: It stays the same, because the charges do not change.
choices.feedback: The charges fix the force, but the distance depends on the energy too: $d = kq_1q_2 : \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. Less energy gives a larger distance.

activities.title: Talk in pairs (2 minutes)
activities.text:
What does *impossible* mean in physics? Think of a ball rolling towards a hill that is too high for it. Is it impossible that it gets over, or only very unlikely? Tell your partner what you think.

Sentence starters

  • I think it is impossible, because …
  • I think it is only unlikely, because …
  • It depends on …

activities.title: Prediction 1: electrons one at a time
activities.prompt: Electrons are sent towards a screen with two very narrow slits, *one electron at a time*. Behind the slits, a detector marks a dot where each electron lands. What picture will thousands of dots make?

choices.text: Two bright stripes, one behind each slit.
choices.feedback: This is what small bullets would do. The experiments show many bright and dark bands instead, an interference pattern, even though the electrons came one at a time.

choices.text: Many bright and dark bands, as for a wave.
choices.feedback: Right. Each electron lands at one point, like a particle, but thousands of dots build up the bright and dark bands of a wave pattern. Something wave-like decides where each electron is likely to land.

choices.text: An even grey spread with no pattern at all.
choices.feedback: After a few dots there is no visible pattern, but after thousands the dots gather into clear bright and dark bands, an interference pattern.

choices.text: No dots, because one electron cannot pass two slits.
choices.feedback: The electrons do arrive, one dot each. And after thousands of them, the dots form bright and dark bands, as if each electron's wave had passed through both slits.

activities.title: Prediction 2: a wall that is too high
activities.prompt: An electron moves towards a thin **energy barrier**. Its kinetic energy is *less* than the energy it would need to get over the top. What does quantum physics say happens?

choices.text: It always bounces back, as a ball would.
choices.feedback: This is the classical answer. For an electron and a thin barrier there is a real chance of passing: for a $1\ \text{eV}$ barrier $0.25\ \text{nm}$ wide, about $7.7\ \%$. This is quantum tunnelling.

choices.text: Sometimes it passes; a wider wall makes it rarer.
choices.feedback: Right. The electron's wave reaches through the barrier, so there is a chance of finding it on the other side. The chance falls very fast with width: about $7.7\ \%$ at $0.25\ \text{nm}$ but only $0.0035\ \%$ at $1.00\ \text{nm}$.

choices.text: It always passes, because an electron is so small.
choices.feedback: Being small does not let it through every time. The chance is only a few per cent for a very thin barrier and falls very fast with width; most electrons bounce back.

choices.text: It waits, collects energy, and then climbs over.
choices.feedback: The electron does not collect extra energy. It passes, when it does, with the energy it had: its wave reaches through the barrier. The chance falls very fast with width.

activities.title: Particle or wave?
activities.prompt:
Discuss with a partner, then write three sentences about the figure with $30$, $300$ and $3000$ electrons. What in the result looks like a particle? What looks like a wave? Can you predict where the next single electron will land?

Word bank

a dot · a band · interference · a pattern builds up · to land · likely / unlikely · probability · at random

Sentence starters

  • Each electron lands …, which looks like a particle.
  • After thousands of electrons, …, which looks like a wave.
  • We cannot predict …, but we can predict …
activities.model: Each electron lands as one small dot at one place, which looks like a particle. After thousands of electrons, the dots build up bright and dark bands, an interference pattern, which looks like a wave. We cannot predict where the next single electron will land, but we can predict where it is likely and unlikely to land: in the bright bands many electrons arrive, in the dark bands almost none.
criteria: The answer says that each electron arrives at one point (particle-like).
The answer says that many electrons form an interference pattern of bands (wave-like).
The answer separates one electron (unpredictable) from the pattern of many (predictable, a probability).
The answer uses at least three words from the word bank.

activities.title: Investigate: how fast does the chance fall?
activities.text: Use the table in *Through the wall*. Look at how the chance of passing changes each time the barrier becomes $0.25\ \text{nm}$ wider.

question.prompt: By what factor does the chance of passing become smaller when the barrier width grows from $0.25\ \text{nm}$ to $0.50\ \text{nm}$? (For example, type $2$ if the chance is halved.)
hints: A factor is found by dividing, not by subtracting.
Divide the larger chance by the smaller one: $7.7\ \% : 0.60\ \%$.
Check the next step too: $0.60\ \% : 0.046\ \%$. Is it about the same factor?

mistakes.feedback: You subtracted ($7.7 - 0.60$). A factor tells how many times smaller the chance is: divide $7.7\ \% : 0.60\ \%$.
You divided the smaller value by the larger one. The chance becomes smaller *by the factor* $7.7\ \% : 0.60\ \% \approx 13$.

question.solution:
**Given:** The chance is $7.7\ \%$ at $0.25\ \text{nm}$ and $0.60\ \%$ at $0.50\ \text{nm}$ (model values). Find the factor.

**Principle:** A factor of change is the ratio of the two values.

**Formula:** $\text{factor} = 7.7\ \% : 0.60\ \%$.

**Unit conversions:** None: both values are percentages.

**Substitution:** $7.7 : 0.60 = 12.8$.

**Answer:** The chance becomes about $13$ times smaller (two significant figures, like the table). The next steps give the same factor: $0.60 : 0.046 \approx 13$ and $0.046 : 0.0035 \approx 13$.

**Reasonableness:** The same factor at every step is the sign of exponential decrease: every extra $0.25\ \text{nm}$ makes passing about $13$ times rarer. Doubling the width does not halve the chance; here it makes it $13$ times smaller.

activities.title: Words of the lesson
Back to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the evidence. Then answer the opening question in one or two sentences: why can the Sun shine, when its protons are far too slow to reach each other?

activities.title: Apply: the wave of a proton in the Sun
activities.prompt: A proton (mass $1.673 \cdot 10^{-27}\ \text{kg}$) at the centre of the Sun has the kinetic energy $1.35\ \text{keV}$. Calculate its de Broglie wavelength in femtometres ($1\ \text{fm} = 10^{-15}\ \text{m}$). Compare it with the classical turning distance, about $1000\ \text{fm}$.
hints: Change the energy to joules: $1\ \text{keV} = 1000\ \text{eV}$ and $1\ \text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$.

mistakes.feedback: You used $1.35\ \text{eV}$ instead of $1.35\ \text{keV}$. One kiloelectronvolt is $1000\ \text{eV}$.
You forgot the factor $2$: $p = \sqrt{2mE_\text{k}}$, because $E_\text{k} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = p^2/(2m)$.
You used the mass of an electron. A proton is about $1840$ times heavier: $m = 1.673 \cdot 10^{-27}\ \text{kg}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** $m = 1.673 \cdot 10^{-27}\ \text{kg}$, $E_\text{k} = 1.35\ \text{keV}$, $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\ \text{J} \cdot \text{s}$. Find the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$.

**Principle:** Every particle has the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda = h/p$. The momentum follows from the kinetic energy, $E_\text{k} = p^2/(2m)$; at this speed classical momentum is accurate.

**Formula:** $p = \sqrt{2mE_\text{k}}$ and $\lambda = h/p = h/\sqrt{2mE_\text{k}}$.

**Unit conversions:** $E_\text{k} = 1.35 \cdot 10^{3}\ \text{eV} \cdot 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\ \text{J/eV} = 2.163 \cdot 10^{-16}\ \text{J}$, and at the end $1\ \text{fm} = 10^{-15}\ \text{m}$.

**Substitution:** $$\begin{aligned} 2mE_\text{k} &= 2 \cdot 1.673 \cdot 10^{-27}\ \text{kg} \\ &\quad \cdot 2.163 \cdot 10^{-16}\ \text{J} \\ &= 7.237 \cdot 10^{-43}\ \text{kg}^2\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2 \\ p &= \sqrt{7.237 \cdot 10^{-43}\ \text{kg}^2\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2} \\ &= 8.507 \cdot 10^{-22}\ \text{kg} \cdot \text{m/s} \\ \lambda &= \frac{6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\ \text{J} \cdot \text{s}}{8.507 \cdot 10^{-22}\ \text{kg} \cdot \text{m/s}} \\ &= 7.79 \cdot 10^{-13}\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$$

**Answer:** $\lambda \approx 7.79 \cdot 10^{-13}\ \text{m} = 779\ \text{fm}$, three significant figures like the energy. It is almost as long as the classical turning distance of about $1000\ \text{fm}$.

**Reasonableness:** The proton is much heavier than the electron of the worked example, but also has more energy; its wavelength, $779\ \text{fm}$, is shorter than the electron's $0.123\ \text{nm} = 123\,000\ \text{fm}$, as expected. Because the wave is about as long as the distance the proton must still cover, its wave reaches into the barrier, and tunnelling becomes possible.

activities.title: Think further: a tennis ball
activities.prompt: A tennis ball ($0.057\ \text{kg}$) flies at $50\ \text{m/s}$. Its de Broglie wavelength is $\lambda = h/(mv) = 2.3 \cdot 10^{-34}\ \text{m}$. Why does nobody ever see a tennis ball diffract or tunnel through the net?

choices.text: Its wavelength is far smaller than any object it meets.
choices.feedback: Right. $2.3 \cdot 10^{-34}\ \text{m}$ is more than $10^{18}$ times smaller than a proton. Wave effects matter only when the wavelength is similar to the size of slits or barriers, and the tunnelling chance through a net is practically zero.

choices.text: Quantum physics is valid only for electrons.
choices.feedback: Quantum physics is valid for everything, also for protons and whole atoms. A tennis ball's wavelength is just far too small to notice.

choices.text: A tennis ball has no wavelength, because it is not moving fast.
choices.feedback: Every moving object has a de Broglie wavelength, $\lambda = h/(mv)$. For the tennis ball it is $2.3 \cdot 10^{-34}\ \text{m}$: real, but far too small to matter.

choices.text: The net is not an energy barrier, so tunnelling is impossible.
choices.feedback: A net that stops a ball acts like a barrier. The point is that the ball's wavelength is so tiny that the chance of tunnelling through it is practically zero.

activities.title: 1. Concept: what the dots tell us
activities.prompt: In a double-slit experiment with single electrons, each electron makes one dot, and thousands of dots make an interference pattern. What does this show?

choices.text: A wave gives the chance of where each one lands.
choices.feedback: Right. One electron lands at one point, but where it lands is random, with probabilities given by the wave. Many electrons show the wave pattern.

choices.text: The electrons push each other into the bands.
choices.feedback: The electrons came one at a time, so they could not push each other. Each electron alone follows the probabilities of its own wave.

choices.text: Each electron splits in two and lands twice.
choices.feedback: Every electron makes exactly one dot: it is never found in two pieces. The pattern of many dots shows the wave.

choices.text: The slits are too wide to stop the electrons.
choices.feedback: The width of the slits is not the point. The surprise is the pattern: bright and dark bands, which only waves make.

activities.title: 2. Tunnelling: a wider barrier
activities.prompt: An electron has a $0.60\ \%$ chance of tunnelling through a barrier $0.50\ \text{nm}$ wide. The barrier is made twice as wide, $1.00\ \text{nm}$, with the same height. What happens to the chance?

choices.text: It halves, to $0.30\ \%$, as the width doubles.
choices.feedback: The chance does not fall in proportion to the width. It falls by the same *factor* for every extra width: in the table, from $0.60\ \%$ to $0.0035\ \%$.

choices.text: It becomes zero: a wide barrier stops it.
choices.feedback: The chance becomes very small, about $0.0035\ \%$, but not zero. Tunnelling becomes rare, not impossible.

choices.text: It falls to about $0.0035\ \%$, far below half.
choices.feedback: Right. The chance falls exponentially: each extra $0.25\ \text{nm}$ makes it about $13$ times smaller, so doubling the width here makes it about $170$ times smaller.

choices.text: It stays the same, because the height is the same.
choices.feedback: The chance depends strongly on the width as well as on the height: it falls from $0.60\ \%$ to about $0.0035\ \%$.

activities.title: 3. The Sun
activities.prompt: Why does fusion happen in the Sun's core, although a typical proton there has only about $1.35\ \text{keV}$ and the barrier is hundreds of $\text{keV}$?

choices.text: The core is hot enough to give protons $720\ \text{keV}$.
choices.feedback: A typical proton has about $1.35\ \text{keV}$, more than $500$ times too little to climb a $720\ \text{keV}$ barrier. Classical physics alone would allow almost no fusion.

choices.text: Protons tunnel, rarely, and there are enormous numbers of them.
choices.feedback: Right. Each meeting of two protons has only a tiny chance to tunnel close enough, but the core contains so many protons that fusion goes on all the time. An average proton waits about $9$ billion years.

choices.text: Protons store energy over many years until they can climb over.
choices.feedback: Protons do not collect energy for a later climb; they collide and exchange energy all the time. Fusion happens by tunnelling with the energy they have.

choices.text: Gravity pulls the protons together against their repulsion.
choices.feedback: Gravity holds the Sun together and keeps the core hot and dense, but between two single protons it is extremely weak. They meet by tunnelling through their electric barrier.

activities.title: 4. Explain: why the Sun shines
activities.prompt:
Explain to a younger student, in four or five sentences, why fusion in the Sun is possible. Use the words *barrier*, *classical physics*, *tunnelling* and *probability*, and at least one number from this unit.

Sentence starters

  • Two protons repel each other, so …
  • In classical physics, a proton with … would …
  • In quantum physics, however, …
  • The probability is very small, but …
  • So the Sun can …
activities.model: Two protons are both positive, so they repel each other, and there is an energy barrier of about $720\ \text{keV}$ before they are close enough to fuse. In classical physics, a proton with a typical energy of $1.35\ \text{keV}$ would turn back about $1000\ \text{fm}$ away and never fuse. In quantum physics, however, a proton also behaves like a wave, and its wave reaches into the barrier. So there is a small probability that two protons tunnel through the barrier and fuse. The probability is very small, but the Sun's core contains so many protons that fusion goes on all the time, and the Sun can shine for billions of years.
criteria: The answer explains the barrier with the repulsion of two positive protons.
The answer contrasts classical physics (no fusion) with tunnelling (a small chance).
The answer explains that a small probability is enough because there are so many protons.
The answer uses all four required words and at least one number from the unit.

activities.text:
Le coin français

Louis de Broglie wrote his famous thesis in French: Recherches sur la théorie des quanta. In French, tunnelling is l'effet tunnel. Listen, repeat, and then say the last sentence to your partner.
